skyline.text: Why Amit Varma obeys the law but calls no gov­ern­ment le­git­i­mate
Ajay Shah re­calls a ver­dict on a fi­nance minister’s ad­vis­ers
How norms kept him from be­com­ing one more dic­ta­tor

brief.head: Legal, not legitimate
brief.text: Stalin’s Russia ran on laws, Ajay Shah said, yet ev­ery­body hated the regime. The NKVD had the legal au­thor­ity to grab you from your bed­room. {098-C03}

brief.head: Brain without fingers
brief.text: Lant Pritchett’s paper calls India a flail­ing state: a bril­liant brain of se­nior of­fi­cials, nerves to the fin­gers sev­ered. Cynical func­tionar­ies, Shah said, are one cause. {098-R05}

brief.head: The passport test
brief.text: Weber’s legal-bureaucratic le­git­i­macy, Shah said, looks like a pass­port of­fice with a known pro­ce­dure: 14 ac­cepted kinds of iden­tity, show any three, no friend in gov­ern­ment needed. {098-J15}

brief.head: Loved until the fall
brief.text: Under an il­le­git­i­mate regime the peo­ple clap and the media praises. Everybody in East Germany loved the Communist Party, Shah said, until the day it fell, friend­less. {098-J10}

brief.head: The knife stays sharp
brief.text: Even an ide­o­logue with a cul­tural pro­gramme needs le­git­i­macy, Shah ar­gued. A le­git­i­mate au­thor­ity can move peo­ple 10 per cent its way and slowly shift so­cial norms. {#tenpercent}

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah and Amit Varma on political legitimacy
lead.head: A monopoly is not a mandate

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 98

play.label: Hear the case in six parts

body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah sat in the sum­mer sun to dis­cuss a sub­ject that, Varma said, is like the sun: “It is ubiq­ui­tous. We ex­pe­ri­ence it every day, and yet we kind of take it for granted, which is the Indian state.” {098-J01}
Shah widened the brief at once. Not just the Indian state, he said: the sub­ject was of great in­ter­est to view­ers “rang­ing from Germany to Mozambique”.

He began with Max Weber, who de­fined the state as the com­mu­nity that achieves and main­tains a mo­nop­oly of vi­o­lence in a given ter­ri­tory. The episode was about the part­ner of that idea: le­git­i­macy.

Legitimacy, Shah said, is the be­lief of the peo­ple that the state has a right to rule over them. Where it ex­ists, peo­ple give the state the ben­e­fit of the doubt, and its laws read­ily turn into so­cial norms. {#define}
Where it is miss­ing, the state must reach into every home by force. “Legitimacy mat­ters be­cause if all you have is co­er­cive power, then you ac­tu­ally have very lit­tle,” he said. {098-C01}

Nor is it only a mat­ter for cit­i­zens. Soldiers, po­lice­men and civil ser­vants must be­lieve in the state too, Shah said, or they roll their eyes at each new edict and the abil­ity to im­ple­ment any­thing fades away. {098-C02}
## Where it comes from

Weber, Shah said, named three sources: tra­di­tion, the charisma of a great leader, and legal, bu­reau­cratic pro­ce­dure under the rule of law. Later schol­ars added a fourth, per­for­mance. {098-C04}
The hosts were record­ing in rural Maharashtra, where, Shah said, there had been twelve hours of power cuts a day for sev­eral days. “That’s not a path to state le­git­i­macy.” {#powercuts}
## What it costs

Without le­git­i­macy, Shah ar­gued, much goes wrong. Spending on polic­ing and sur­veil­lance bal­loons, in­ter­per­sonal vi­o­lence rises, peo­ple start lying to the state, tal­ent and cap­i­tal leave, and small prob­lems snow­ball into big ones. {098-C06}

Even a ruler who cares only for him­self should want le­git­i­macy, he said, be­cause co­er­cion is costly and a le­git­i­mate gov­ern­ment col­lects more tax. In India, he said, peo­ple “move en­tire in­dus­tries into cash ac­tiv­i­ties in order to avoid the GST”. {#cash}
A smart ruler, in other words, cul­ti­vates le­git­i­macy in order to ex­tract more, not less. {098-C07}

Shah, ad­mit­ting that at 59 his mem­ory was start­ing to fade, then read from notes a check­list for any politi­cian or civil ser­vant: trans­parency, ac­count­abil­ity, pro­ce­dural fair­ness, con­sul­ta­tion, de­cen­tral­i­sa­tion, per­for­mance, vis­i­ble ex­per­tise, re­spect for norms and telling the truth. {098-J03}
## Varma’s four thoughts

Then it was Varma’s turn. Compliance, or the ab­sence of dis­sent, should not be mis­taken for le­git­i­macy, he warned. He him­self con­sid­ers no gov­ern­ment le­git­i­mate, just as he re­jects the so­cial con­tract, since he never signed one. {098-C11}

Most Indians, he ar­gued, thrive de­spite a par­a­sitic state and are ap­a­thetic about its le­git­i­macy, be­cause power and ac­count­abil­ity have come apart. Voting, he said, has be­come tribal loy­alty, like sup­port­ing Manchester United or Liverpool. {098-J14}

The Constitution, Varma said, was more lib­eral than the so­ci­ety it gov­erned. {098-C13} Politics has since caught up with so­ci­ety, and an English-speaking elite, he ar­gued, can­not de­clare a gov­ern­ment il­le­git­i­mate just be­cause it dis­likes its val­ues.
The real fight, he said, is in the mar­ket­place of ideas, and that needs free­dom. “Legitimacy is im­pos­si­ble with­out free­dom.” {098-C14}

He al­lowed that he was per­haps cast­ing a cyn­i­cal eye on the whole episode. It was still im­por­tant, he said, to look at all these frame­works of le­git­i­macy and to as­pire to­wards a bet­ter world.

second.label: Roving and stationary
second.head: A bandit with prospects
second.deck: Mancur Olson’s bandits show why even a selfish ruler wants legitimacy

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Mancur Olson’s two bandits

body: Amit Varma reached for two terms coined by the econ­o­mist Mancur Olson. A rov­ing ban­dit de­stroys a vil­lage com­pletely, be­cause he comes and goes. A sta­tion­ary ban­dit in­tends to stay and keep rob­bing, so he has to let the peo­ple pros­per. {098-R06}
Perversely enough, Varma said, this is pub­lic choice logic at work: even a ban­dit should at least try to be a le­git­i­mate one. {098-C08}

Ajay Shah car­ried the idea fur­ther. Under a ban­dit with le­git­i­macy, vil­lagers im­prove their land, start shops and busi­nesses and build bet­ter homes. If the ban­dit robs and pil­lages as he likes, the peo­ple are more likely to just dig holes in the ground and hide their gold. {#gold}

quote.text: Even if you’re a ban­dit, it is in your in­ter­est to at least try to be a le­git­i­mate ban­dit.

third.head: Howzat for legitimacy?

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on elections as cricket matches

body: A lot of peo­ple see pol­i­tics as a game, Ajay Shah said, and the media breath­lessly re­ports elec­tion re­sults as it would a cricket match.
But elec­tions now hap­pen in many coun­tries. Vladimir Putin holds them, he pointed out, and wins with 85 per cent of the vote share. {#putin}

Populist regimes that pur­sue only their base, he said, can keep win­ning and still face a gap in le­git­i­macy. Nor do 320 seats make a gov­ern­ment fully le­git­i­mate, what­ever the media shouts. {#seats}

Legitimacy lies in­side people’s minds: “You have to go into the eye rolling of the civil ser­vant or the cit­i­zen when one more fatwa comes from high above. That’s le­git­i­macy, and you don’t get that merely by win­ning elec­tions.” {098-C05}

p2.title: The right to rule
p2.deck: Ajay Shah builds the idea of legitimacy from Max Weber up; Amit Varma asks whether it matters in India

from1.head: A monopoly is not a mandate

quote.text: So state le­git­i­macy is not just about the eyes of the pop­u­lace, it is also in the eyes of the state.

box.title: Ajay’s one recommendation
box.text: Max Weber de­fined the state as the com­mu­nity that achieves and main­tains a mo­nop­oly of vi­o­lence, and gave le­git­i­macy as its part­ner idea. Ajay Shah’s one rec­om­men­da­tion was Weber’s *Politics as a Vocation*, “one of the great books of the world”. {098-R01}

sections.label: The idea
sections.head: Believed, not merely obeyed
sections.caption: what legitimacy means
body: Amit Varma began with def­i­ni­tions, since a word can carry one mean­ing in ev­ery­day par­lance and a more fixed one in po­lit­i­cal sci­ence. Ajay Shah’s an­swer: le­git­i­macy is the be­lief of the peo­ple that the state has a right to rule over them. {#define}

It is “a very messy, soft con­struct”, he said. Told to drive on the left side of the road, a cit­i­zen of a le­git­i­mate state as­sumes there is prob­a­bly some merit to it, and the rule be­comes a con­ven­tion.

Even an odd edict, such as wear­ing blue caps on Tuesday, is more likely to be fol­lowed where there is re­spect. Without that good faith the state must live by force, and “you can’t live by vi­o­lence every day”. {098-C01}
## Inside the ma­chine

In an il­le­git­i­mate state, Shah said, a po­lice­man reads each new clause in the IPC as a chance for a new pro­tec­tion racket. Handed a UIDAI-backed sys­tem for the PDS, a civil ser­vant gig­gles in­side and tells his bud­dies how to by­pass it.
The func­tionar­ies of the state have to be­lieve in its shared mis­sion, virtue and com­pe­tence, he said; oth­er­wise the abil­ity to im­ple­ment any­thing fades away. {098-C02}

~ Nor is power the same thing. Varma called this the gap be­tween po­lit­i­cal au­thor­ity and po­lit­i­cal le­git­i­macy. Once the state can break down any door with­out fac­ing ma­chine-gun re­turn fire, Shah said, Weber’s first level is as­sured. “Then what?”

quote.text: So state le­git­i­macy is not just about the eyes of the pop­u­lace, it is also in the eyes of the state.

sections.label: The four sources
sections.head: Four roads to respect
sections.caption: where legitimacy comes from
body: Max Weber, Ajay Shah said, taught three di­rec­tions from which le­git­i­macy arises. The first is tra­di­tion. When Aurangzeb be­came em­peror, he re­ceived the re­spect that had been given to the Mughal Empire for hun­dreds of years. Patriarchy gets a cer­tain re­spect for free, be­cause it has al­ways been there.

The sec­ond is charisma. Napoleon was not part of the tra­di­tional sys­tem, since the French Revolution had killed off France’s dy­nas­tic rule, yet he achieved le­git­i­macy through the sheer power of his char­ac­ter.
In India, Shah said, the clos­est ex­am­ple is Nehru, whose au­thor­ity was moral and in­tel­lec­tual, “not merely that I have the big stick”. {#moral}
When Shah twice com­pared the state to a com­pany, Amit Varma scolded him on be­half of a good friend, one Dr Shah, who keeps telling him a coun­try is not like a com­pany.
## Rules and re­sults

The third source is legal, bu­reau­cratic pro­ce­dure under the rule of law: rules that are thought through and con­sid­ered fair, so that get­ting a pass­port means fol­low­ing a due process, not phon­ing a friend in gov­ern­ment.

~ Later schol­ars added a fourth: per­for­mance. Keep the peace and make the po­lice and courts work, Shah said, and you are on a path to le­git­i­macy. China’s Communist Party earned re­spect by de­liv­er­ing a 10x of per capita GDP. {#tenx}

quote.text: That a state earns le­git­i­macy by get­ting shit done.

sections.label: The cost
sections.head: What distrust costs a state
sections.caption: what breaks without legitimacy
body: Amit Varma put the hard case. An au­thor­i­tar­ian who has achieved the mo­nop­oly of vi­o­lence might ask why le­git­i­macy should mat­ter to him. Ajay Shah an­swered with a chain of harms.

First, co­er­cion. The gov­ern­ment pours money into its co­er­cive or­gans and builds a sur­veil­lance state, which Shah called a dead­weight loss. To watch ev­ery­one, he said, “you may end up with like one in every three cit­i­zens being a se­cu­rity ap­pa­ra­tus mem­ber”. {#threecitizens}
Interpersonal vi­o­lence rises too, and Shah counted vi­o­lence by the po­lice and the hang­man as part of it. {098-C06}
## A state gone blind

Next, in­for­ma­tion. People cheer­fully vol­un­teer in­for­ma­tion to a le­git­i­mate state, Shah said; to an il­le­git­i­mate one they lie. Its abil­ity to see, in the sense of James C. Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*, goes down. {098-J09}

Brain drain and cap­i­tal flight fol­low, be­cause fewer peo­ple will tie their lives to a state they do not trust. And small sparks, such as a Jat ag­i­ta­tion in Haryana, can grow big in un­ex­pected ways when no­body gives the state the ben­e­fit of the doubt.
~ The end of the chain, Shah said, is “the whole en­chi­lada”: the sta­bil­ity of the regime it­self. A le­git­i­mate state reaches be­yond its base to a wide spec­trum of peo­ple.

quote.text: A good so­ci­ety is one where there are low lev­els of in­ter­per­sonal vi­o­lence.

sections.label: Public choice
sections.head: Selfish reasons to be liked
sections.caption: the selfish case for legitimacy
body: Public choice the­ory as­sumes that the peo­ple who run the state are self-interested ac­tors who do not care what a good so­ci­ety is. So Ajay Shah set de­cency aside and ar­gued from their own in­ter­est.

Coercion is ex­pen­sive and painful, he said. A more le­git­i­mate gov­ern­ment finds greater ac­cep­tance of its taxes. Under the GST, by con­trast, whole in­dus­tries have moved into cash as peo­ple do all they can to avoid it. {#cash}
Legitimacy also buys sta­bil­ity, and a brit­tle regime that lives by vi­o­lence every day can­not ex­tract more re­sources. A smart ruler, Shah con­cluded, would cul­ti­vate it. {098-C07}
## The ideologue’s cal­cu­la­tion

Then Shah took a ruler who wants nei­ther money nor ar­bi­trary power, only to push a cul­tural or na­tion­al­ist pro­gramme. Such a ruler still needs a state that works, and an il­le­git­i­mate state is blunt: civil ser­vants roll their eyes and only por­tray com­pli­ance. {098-C09}
A pro­gramme forced on peo­ple makes them hate it more every day, he said. Legitimacy, by con­trast, grows the na­tion rather than shrink­ing it.
~ Amit Varma, in mock out­rage, ac­cused Shah of teach­ing dem­a­gogues to think ra­tio­nally, and asked how any gov­ern­ment might ac­tu­ally earn le­git­i­macy.

quote.text: So an en­light­ened king, an en­light­ened state would want to ex­tract more for her­self, not less.

sections.label: The checklist
sections.head: Show your working, minister
sections.caption: a toolkit for earning legitimacy
body: This, Ajay Shah said, is where the episode goes from ab­stract ideas to ac­tion. He read his check­list for every civil ser­vant and politi­cian from notes. {098-J03}

Transparency comes first: ex­pert com­mit­tee re­ports, pub­lic de­bate, and draft laws shown be­fore they are en­acted. Then ac­count­abil­ity: griev­ance re­dres­sal, audit and low cor­rup­tion, so that no in­come tax of­fi­cer or po­lice­man can harm peo­ple at will.

Procedural fair­ness means laws known in ad­vance and en­forced equally, with a fair hear­ing be­fore a neu­tral judge. Shah in­vented an ob­scure rule to show the al­ter­na­tive: “Did you know that on cam­era you can­not be con­sum­ing Diet Coke? It has to be Diet Pepsi.” {098-J04}

Consultation means open con­sul­ta­tions and town halls, though not plebiscites. Decentralisation pushes the most power to cities, where peo­ple can see their side­walks re­paired. And per­for­mance counts: from 1991 to 2011, he said, the Indian state wore a halo be­cause it de­liv­ered a 4x of GDP growth. {#gdp4x}
## No tablets of stone
Expertise must be vis­i­ble. Edicts can­not sim­ply come down from the top of a moun­tain like Moses’s Ten Commandments, Shah said: “that earns no re­spect.” {098-J06}
~ Respect for norms and telling the truth com­plete the list. Propaganda, he warned, is cor­ro­sive, be­cause peo­ple dis­cover that they are being lied to.

quote.text: That I may dis­agree with the out­come, but I want to see that you have the brains, you have the smarts.

sections.label: Amit’s dissent
sections.head: Obedient, but not convinced
sections.caption: why legitimacy may not matter in India
body: Amit Varma first warned against mis­tak­ing com­pli­ance, or the ab­sence of dis­sent, for le­git­i­macy. Then he zoomed out in four steps.

First, him­self. He will never con­sider any gov­ern­ment le­git­i­mate, he said, just as he re­jects the so­cial con­tract. “I have never agreed to sign a so­cial con­tract.” He obeys the law to stay out of jail, for prac­ti­cal rea­sons, not eth­i­cal ones. {098-C11}
Second, so­ci­ety. For most Indians the rule of law does not exist, he said; they thrive de­spite the state, as the title of Gurcharan Das’s *India Grows at Night* says. {098-R07}

Power and ac­count­abil­ity have come apart, he ar­gued, be­cause India lacks de­cen­tral­i­sa­tion: the peo­ple he votes for can­not change his life, and those who can do not need his vote. {098-C12}
## Topsoil and the bat­tle of ideas

Third, his­tory. The Constitution was more lib­eral than a so­ci­ety driven by caste, sex­ism and misog­yny. Ambedkar, Varma said, spoke of vil­lages as dens of ig­no­rance and saw the Constitution as just a top­soil. {098-J13}
The missed task was to spread lib­eral val­ues bot­tom-up. Now pol­i­tics has caught up with so­ci­ety. “You and I are the fringe,” he told Ajay Shah.

~ Fourth, free­dom. Legitimacy needs an open con­test of ideas, he said, and there is no level play­ing field if you freeze the opposition’s bank ac­counts and stop them from cam­paign­ing. {#bankaccounts}

quote.text: Our con­sti­tu­tion was a con­sti­tu­tion cre­ated by an ini­tially un­elected lib­eral elite and im­posed on an il­lib­eral so­ci­ety.
The peo­ple I vote for don’t have power to change my life. And the peo­ple who have power to change my life don’t need my vote.

p3.title: Stories of the state
p3.deck: A put-down, a puzzle and a prime minister’s restraint

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on why governments need visible expertise
stories.head: Economists? Then I’m a dancer
body: Soon after Yashwant Sinha be­came Finance Minister, Ajay Shah re­called, he shared a con­fer­ence panel with the econ­o­mist Jagdish Bhagwati. {098-S01}
Bhagwati help­fully turned to the new min­is­ter with ad­vice. Expertise re­ally mat­ters, he said: get the best peo­ple in the coun­try into your gov­ern­ment as your ad­vis­ers.

Sinha named a cou­ple of peo­ple who were with him and would take part in his rul­ing ar­range­ment. Bhagwati’s reply be­came fa­mous: “If they are econ­o­mists, then I’m a Bharatanatyam dancer.” {#natyam}

Shah called it a funny mo­ment in Indian his­tory, but he told it as part of his check­list for earn­ing le­git­i­macy. Edicts need vis­i­ble rea­son­ing, he said, be­cause peo­ple may dis­agree with an out­come but still want to see that a gov­ern­ment has the brains. {098-C10}
~ Teams, ex­per­tise and com­pe­tence, Shah said: these things earn le­git­i­macy.
stories.why: A gov­ern­ment earns le­git­i­macy partly by vis­i­bly as­sem­bling com­pe­tent teams. Citizens and ex­perts judge it by whom it chooses to lis­ten to, and ad­vis­ers who are ex­perts only in name drain its cred­i­bil­ity.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Jagdish Bhagwati’s put-down

stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells a thought experiment from Jason Brennan
stories.head: Same blow, different uniform
body: Amit Varma’s rec­om­men­da­tion came with a puz­zle. The book was the philoso­pher Jason Brennan’s *When All Else Fails: The Ethics of Resistance to State Injustice*, which the hosts’ mu­tual friend Abhinav Singh had urged him to read. {098-R02}
It poses a two-part thought ex­per­i­ment. You are walk­ing down the street and some ran­dom man starts hit­ting a beg­gar. Your first in­stinct is to in­ter­vene.

Now make the man a po­lice­man with a lathi. You stay away. It is, Varma said, “not just a ques­tion of au­thor­ity, but also a ques­tion of le­git­i­macy”: in a way, you are ac­cord­ing le­git­i­macy to the po­lice­man be­cause of his uni­form. {098-S02}

~ Varma said he did not want to take a po­si­tion. Brennan had been his guest on *The Seen and the Unseen* five or six years ago; Varma threw many coun­ter­fac­tu­als at him and was blown away by the clar­ity of his think­ing.
stories.why: Our in­stincts qui­etly grant the state’s agents a moral li­cence we would never give a pri­vate per­son. The uni­form does eth­i­cal work in our heads, which shows le­git­i­macy to be a be­lief peo­ple hold, not just a legal sta­tus.
stories.postscript: In that con­ver­sa­tion, Brennan re­ferred to a book by Michael Huemer that is just on state le­git­i­macy. {#huemer}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the policeman and the beggar

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on norms as a source of power
stories.head: The power Nehru left unused
body: Looking for India’s clos­est ex­am­ple of charis­matic le­git­i­macy, Ajay Shah chose Jawaharlal Nehru: a well-loved fig­ure, re­spected all over India, who of course won elec­tions, “but that’s the least of it”.
When Nehru said “guys, we should think about some­thing”, peo­ple took him se­ri­ously. His au­thor­ity, Shah said, was moral and in­tel­lec­tual. {#moral}

Later, Shah re­turned to Nehru to make a point about re­straint. The Indian state was quite lim­ited at the time, he said, and there was plenty Nehru could have done. “He could lit­er­ally have gone down the path of be­com­ing one more third world dic­ta­tor.” He did not. {098-S03}

~ Norms, in Shah’s ac­count, are an in­tan­gi­ble path to charis­matic power. Using hard power crudely, and de­stroy­ing norms sim­ply be­cause one can, hin­ders le­git­i­macy. People want to see a nice guy, he said, a grace­ful per­son.

quote.text: There was de­cency, there were norms, there were many things that are just not done, and that earns re­spect, that earns le­git­i­macy.

quiz.q: What did Jagdish Bhagwati say he would be if the new finance minister’s advisers were economists?
quiz.a: A Bharatanatyam dancer, as he told Yashwant Sinha on a con­fer­ence panel.

quiz.q: According to Max Weber, as Ajay Shah explained, what are the three sources of legitimacy?
quiz.a: Tradition, charisma, and legal, bu­reau­cratic pro­ce­dure under the rule of law.

quiz.q: Which leader did Ajay Shah cite to show that winning elections does not confer legitimacy?
quiz.a: Vladimir Putin, who holds elec­tions and wins about 85 per cent of the vote.

quiz.q: In Mancur Olson’s terms, why does a stationary bandit let the village prosper?
quiz.a: Because he in­tends to stay and keep rob­bing, so some­thing must be left.

quiz.q: Why does Amit Varma refuse to accept the social contract?
quiz.a: A con­tract needs vol­un­tary con­sent be­tween par­ties, and he never signed one.

quiz.q: In Jason Brennan’s thought experiment, what do most people do when a policeman beats a beggar?
quiz.a: They stay away, ac­cord­ing the uni­formed man a le­git­i­macy they would deny a stranger.

A ca­pa­ble brain at the top, cut off from its fin­gers
Pure waste, as with money poured into sur­veil­lance

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 98. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Max Weber (Ernst Gottmann, public domain); Napoleon (Jacques-Louis David, public domain); B. R. Ambedkar (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Gurcharan Das (Gurcharan Das, CC BY 3.0).

shelf.title: Politics as a Vocation
shelf.creator: Max Weber
shelf.why: Ajay calls it one of the great books of the world and says ev­ery­body should read it.

shelf.title: When All Else Fails: The Ethics of Resistance to State Injustice
shelf.creator: Jason Brennan
shelf.why: It poses the po­lice­man-versus-stranger thought ex­per­i­ment, which forces you to ask why we grant state agents moral cover.

shelf.title: The Problem of Political Authority
shelf.creator: Michael Huemer
shelf.why: Amit says it is a book en­tirely about state le­git­i­macy and that lis­ten­ers should also read it.

shelf.title: Resisting State Injustice (Episode 120 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: They dis­cussed state le­git­i­macy di­rectly in that episode.

shelf.title: Is India a Flailing State?
shelf.creator: Lant Pritchett
shelf.why: Pritchett’s image of the Indian state as a world-class brain of se­nior of­fi­cials whose nerves to the limbs are cut, so noth­ing changes on the ground.

shelf.title: The Logic of Collective Action
shelf.creator: Mancur Olson
shelf.why: Olson’s ac­count of ‘con­cen­trated ben­e­fits and dif­fuse costs’: why small, or­gan­ised in­ter­est groups beat the large, un­or­gan­ised pub­lic.

shelf.title: India Grows at Night
shelf.creator: Gurcharan Das
shelf.why: Amit calls the title great be­cause it cap­tures how Indians live and thrive de­spite a dys­func­tional, ex­trac­tive state, which makes the ques­tion of its le­git­i­macy al­most be­side the point.

shelf.title: Understanding the State (Episode 25)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The foun­da­tion of the show’s think­ing on gov­ern­ment: the state is a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence that acts through co­er­cion, so every in­ter­ven­tion, paid for by taxes, must be jus­ti­fied.

shelf.title: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on mar­ket fail­ure in its pre­cise tech­ni­cal sense (pub­lic goods, ex­ter­nal­i­ties and the rest) and on the nar­row con­di­tions under which the state may in­ter­vene, con­di­tions that are nec­es­sary but not suf­fi­cient.

shelf.title: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Explains that politi­cians and bu­reau­crats re­spond to in­cen­tives like ev­ery­one else, so the state is no benev­o­lent beast and gov­ern­ment fail­ure is far more com­mon than mar­ket fail­ure.

shelf.title: Separation of Powers (Episode 91) and Rules, Not Discretion (Episode 92) of Everything is Everything
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why fus­ing leg­isla­tive, ex­ec­u­tive and ju­di­cial pow­ers, as Indian reg­u­la­tors do, is so dan­ger­ous.

shelf.title: India Needs Decentralization (Episode 47)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case for sub­sidiar­ity in a coun­try as large and var­ied as India: do as lit­tle as pos­si­ble at the Union level and push power down to cities, where peo­ple can see and talk to the of­fi­cials re­spon­si­ble for their side­walks.

shelf.title: Why I Am a Free Speech Absolutist (Episode 88)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s case for free speech: why the Indian Constitution doesn’t re­ally pro­tect it, why Nehru’s First Amendment was a mis­take to be un­der­stood in con­text, and why le­git­i­macy needs an open mar­ket­place of ideas.

laughs.text: Amit’s open­ing: they are sit­ting in the sum­mer sun to dis­cuss a sub­ject that is ‘like the sun. You know, it is ubiq­ui­tous. We ex­pe­ri­ence it every day, and yet we kind of take it for granted, which is the Indian state.’ Ajay widens the scope: ‘Not just the Indian state. So this is of great in­ter­est to our view­ers rang­ing from Germany to Mozambique.’

After Ajay twice com­pares the state to a cor­po­ra­tion, Amit scolds him: ‘a good friend of mine, I don’t know if you know him, Dr. Shah, keeps telling me that a coun­try is not like a com­pany... Stop it, sir. Dr. Shah will be very angry with you.’

Ajay reads his le­git­i­macy check­list from notes ‘be­cause I’m 59 years old, my mem­ory is start­ing to fade.’ Amit tells the ‘gen­tle listener’ that Ajay nor­mally does the whole show from mem­ory while Amit glances at his phone, so ‘he’s fi­nally show­ing that he’s human in some ways.’
Ajay’s made-up ob­scure reg­u­la­tion to il­lus­trate pro­ce­dural un­fair­ness: ‘Did you know that on cam­era you can­not be con­sum­ing Diet Coke? It has to be Diet Pepsi.’

On why gov­ern­ments must show their rea­son­ing, Ajay says edicts can’t just come down ‘from the top of a moun­tain that you know Moses went and met God and these are the ten com­mand­ments. Okay, that earns no re­spect.’
Bertolt Brecht: Amit re­calls the poem say­ing that if a gov­ern­ment has lost the con­fi­dence of the peo­ple, it should just elect a new peo­ple.
East Germany: ‘ev­ery­body in East Germany loved the Communist Party until the day the com­mu­nist party fell, and then sud­denly you re­al­ized that the Communist Party had ab­so­lutely no friends.’
The car­toon of two wolves and a sheep vot­ing on what to have for din­ner. Amit uses it to argue that you can’t just be a democ­racy; you need a con­sti­tu­tional bedrock and a re­pub­lic.
